text:
The year I lived in the house on Prospect Street, we all believed we were conducting experiments on one another. We were graduate students, or adjacent to graduate students, and we treated our own lives the way we treated our coursework—with excessive annotation and very little commitment to any single conclusion.

Carl had the ground-floor room because he'd been there longest and because, as he liked to say, his spine required it. He was writing a dissertation on municipal water systems that he described, at parties, as "a history of thirst," which made people want to talk to him and then, within minutes, want to talk to someone else. I loved him in the way you love a relative whose flaws you've memorized so thoroughly they've become comforts. I knew he would interrupt. I knew he would forget the utility bill and then produce a brilliant lecture on the sociology of electricity. I knew he would leave his bike unlocked and grieve theatrically when it was stolen, twice.

Martin lived in the back bedroom and was the only one of us with a real job, at a lab across the river, which gave him an aura of adulthood he exploited shamelessly. He bought good olive oil. He pronounced my name correctly on the first try, which should not have mattered and did. Lizzy had the attic room and a rotating cast of ambitions: ceramics, then translation, then something involving archival photographs of glaciers. She was the kind of beautiful that made strangers helpful. Johan was not technically a resident but was present so often—Carl's oldest friend, visiting from Copenhagen for a semester, then another, then indefinitely—that his toothbrush simply appeared in our bathroom one day, the way weather arrives.

I should say that I came to the house wounded, though I would not have used that word then. I had left a program in another state, and a man in that program, under circumstances I described as "mutual," a word that did a great deal of unearned labor in those years. I arrived with two suitcases and a belief that I was done with complication. I was twenty-six. I thought complication was a country you could emigrate from.

The first thing that happened was Martin. It happened slowly and then in a single evening, over a pot of his good olive oil and some pasta, while Carl was at a conference and Lizzy was at her kiln. Martin asked me about the man I'd left, and I told him the truth for the first time—not the "mutual" version—and he listened without performing listening, which is rarer than you'd think. Afterward we sat on the back steps and he said, "You don't have to be interesting for me," which remains the most romantic sentence anyone has ever said to me, and also, I came to understand, a warning.

The thing about Martin was that he was kind without being curious. He loved me the way you love a view from a window you've gotten used to: warmly, and without ever going outside into it. For a long time I mistook this for peace. I had come from a relationship that was all weather, and Martin was climate. I stopped writing the essay I'd been carrying around for two years and started making soups. Carl noticed before I did. "You've gotten quiet," he said, in his blunt municipal way. "You used to argue with me about everything. Now you just hand me things."

Meanwhile, Lizzy was falling apart so gracefully that it took us months to see it. The glaciers had stopped holding her interest; the photographs all looked, she said, like the same photograph. She took to sleeping in the afternoons and appearing at dinner with the radiant, slightly stunned air of someone returning from a journey. It was Johan who finally said it, one night when she had gone to bed at eight. "She is not all right." The room rearranged itself around the sentence. We'd all been treating her decline as a personality quirk, because the house ran on the fiction that everyone in it was basically fine.

I want to be honest about what happened next, because I wasn't, then.

It began with Johan and me driving Lizzy to a doctor's appointment Martin was too busy for and Carl was too squeamish to acknowledge. It began, really, in the car, where Johan told me about a coastline in Denmark where his grandmother had lived, where the land and the sea were still arguing about their boundary, and I thought: *he describes things the way I describe things.* Recognition is more dangerous than attraction. Attraction you can dismiss. Recognition feels like fate doing you a favor.

Nothing happened for a long time. That is the truth, and it is also a lie, because everything happened; it just happened in glances and in the kitchen, in the way he'd read aloud a sentence from his manuscript and look to me for the verdict, in the way I began saving my best thoughts of the day for eleven o'clock, when he came home and I was somehow always making tea. Martin was in bed by ten-thirty. He had a real job. I had tea, and a Dane, and a conscience I kept sending to its room like a disobedient child.

Carl figured it out first, because Carl, for all his soliloquies about reservoirs, was the most attentive person in the house. He didn't confront me. He did something worse: he became kind to me. He did my dishes. He asked, gently, how my essay was going, knowing full well I hadn't touched it. His kindness was a mirror, and I hated him for it, briefly and intensely, the way you can only hate someone whose house you live in.

The betrayal, when it came, was not the one you're expecting. Or it was, and it wasn't. Johan and I never crossed the line I had drawn in my head—the line was real, I want that on the record—but I learned, in April, that he had crossed it with Lizzy. In February. During the very weeks I was driving her to appointments, making broth. She told me herself, in the attic, sitting among her identical glaciers, with a strange relief, as if I were a priest rather than a person. "I didn't know where else to put it," she said. She meant the secret, which had compounded, the way secrets do, into something with interest.

What undid me was not the betrayal of my almost-love for Johan. It was the discovery that everyone had been protecting a different fiction. Johan had been kind to Lizzy in her illness and had let kindness slide into something else. Lizzy had confessed to me not because I was safe but because I was compromised—she knew, the way everyone in that house knew everything, about the eleven-o'clock teas—and confessing neutralized us both. And Carl had known about all of it for weeks and had said nothing, had instead done my dishes, and when I demanded to know why, he said, with a sincerity that ended something between us and began something better, "Because I was afraid you'd leave, and you're the only one who argues with me."

I did leave, eventually. But first came the strangest summer of my life, the summer we all stayed anyway, because leases and dissertations and inertia are stronger than hurt feelings. Johan went back to Copenhagen in June, leaving the toothbrush and a manuscript I never read. Lizzy got a real diagnosis and real help, and started making small clay figures, hundreds of them, of a woman sleeping, each slightly different, which I thought were the best things she'd ever made. She gave me one. The woman's face is not peaceful, exactly, but she is clearly dreaming.

Martin and I ended the way we began, quietly, on the back steps. He said he had known for months that I was somewhere else, and I asked why he'd never fought for me, and he said, honestly, "I don't fight for things. I thought you liked that about me." I had. I had liked it until I understood it wasn't peace; it was absence with good manners. He cried, briefly, and I cried, and then we discussed who would keep the good olive oil, and I let him have it, which I regretted and then didn't.

It was Carl who drove me to the bus station in August, who carried my suitcases—the same two, minus a few illusions, plus a clay figure wrapped in a T-shirt. He talked the whole way about his dissertation, which had somehow become a book about how cities decide what their citizens deserve. At the curb he hugged me with his bad spine and said, "Write the essay. Stop making soup." I said I would. He said, "You're going to write about us, aren't you." I said absolutely not. We both knew.

And here is the thing I couldn't have told you then, standing on that curb: the house on Prospect Street was the experiment, and we were all both the scientists and the subjects, and the data was a mess, and the conclusions were wrong, and I would not trade a single afternoon of it. Not the teas at eleven, not the broth, not even the attic with its terrible honest glaciers. I had arrived believing I was done with complication, and I left understanding that complication is not a country. It is the water supply. It runs under everything, and you do not emigrate from it; you only learn, finally, where the pipes are.
